'''Mary Fanett Wheeler''' (born December 28, 1938)<ref name=scott>{{cite web|last=Riddle|first=Larry|title=Mary F. Wheeler|url=http://www.agnesscott.edu/lriddle/women/mwheeler.htm|work=Biographies of Women Mathematicians|accessdate=31 January 2012}}</ref> is an [[Americans|American]] [[mathematician]]. She is known for her work on [[numerical methods]] for [[partial differential equations]], including [[domain decomposition method]]s.

In 1998, Wheeler was elected a member of the [[National Academy of Engineering]] for "the computer simulation of subsurface flow and the underlying mathematical algorithms".<ref>{{Cite web | url=https://www.nae.edu/27549/Dr-Mary-F-Wheeler | title=Dr. Mary F. Wheeler }}</ref>

In 2009 she was awarded the [[Theodore von Kármán Prize]] by the [[Society for Industrial and Applied Mathematics]] (SIAM).<ref>{{Cite web |title=UT Austin professor honored with prestigious mathematics award |date=30 June 2009 |url=http://www.siam.org/about/news-siam.php?id=1579 |publisher=Society for Industrial and Applied Mathematics |accessdate=30 November 2012 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170111084528/http://www.siam.org/about/news-siam.php?id=1579 |archive-date=11 January 2017 |url-status=dead }}</ref>

== Personal background ==
Mary Fanett Wheeler was born on December 28, 1938, in [[Cuero, Texas]].<ref name=scott/> She earned a double major in social sciences and mathematics from the [[University of Texas]] in 1960, and a [[Master's degree]] in 1963.<ref name=scott/>  She did her masters thesis on the [[Alternating direction implicit method|Peaceman-Rachford method]], and later went on to do her [[Ph.D.]] under Rachford at [[Rice University]] in 1971.<ref name=scw>{{cite news|last=Murphy|first=John|title=Playing the numbers game|url=http://www.scientific-computing.com/features/feature.php?feature_id=120|accessdate=17 October 2013|newspaper=Scientific Computing World|date=March–April 2003}}{{Dead link|date=January 2026 |bot=InternetArchiveBot }}</ref>

== Professional background ==
Wheeler studies [[finite element method|finite element analysis]] and porous media problems with applications in engineering, oil-field exploitation, and the cleaning up of environmental pollution.<ref name=scw/> Her early work consisted of fundamental contributions to [[finite element method]]s and [[numerical analysis]].<ref name = scw/>  She then moved into porous media problems, using her numerical expertise to study problems in the oil industry such as managing oil-field extraction.<ref name = scw/>  She also studies environmental problems such as cleaning up underground reservoirs, spills of toxic waste, and [[carbon sequestration|carbon dioxide sequestration]].<ref name=scw/>  In addition, Wheeler has worked with the [[United States Army Corps of Engineers]] on environmental impact in the [[Chesapeake Bay]], [[Delaware Bay]], and [[Florida Bay]].<ref name=scw/>

On the matter of pure versus applied math, Wheeler has been noted to say "To me it is important to see your work used. I do abstract things as well, and I don't know if I will live to see them applied."<ref name=scw/>

Wheeler worked at the [[Rice University]] from 1971 to 1995, with a two-year hiatus at [[University of Houston]] from 1988 to 1990.<ref name=scw/>  In 1995 she moved to the [[University of Texas at Austin]] (UT) where she served as the director of the [[Center for Subsurface Modeling]]<ref>(See https://www.oden.utexas.edu/research/centers-groups/csm/)</ref> at the [[Oden Institute for Computational Engineering and Sciences]].<ref>{{Cite web |url=http://users.ices.utexas.edu/~mfw/ |title=Mary Fanett Wheeler |work=The Institute for Computational Science and Engineering |publisher=The University of Texas at Austin |accessdate=30 November 2012}}</ref> She retired from UT in 2024.<ref name=WheelerRetires>{{cite web|accessdate=March 25, 2025
|url=https://cockrell.utexas.edu/news/archive/10070-computational-sciences-pioneer-mary-wheeler-retires
|title= Computational Sciences Pioneer Mary Wheeler Retires |date=October 10, 2024|publisher=Cockrell School of Engineering, University of Texas at Austin}},</ref>

Wheeler is a Professional [[Engineer]] registered with the State of Texas since 1999.<ref name=cv>{{cite web|last=Wheeler|first=Mary|title=Resume|url=http://users.ices.utexas.edu/~mfw/vitae.html|accessdate=13 October 2013}}<br/><br/>Note: if the [[hyperlink]] displayed as "Resume" in the above "ref" has become a [[dead link]], then ... this URL : https://www.oden.utexas.edu/people/directory/mary-wheeler-354/ might be helpful ... as it seems to be more recently updated. (On the other hand, it might have been updated *before* "She retired from UT in 2024.")</ref>  In 1989, she gave the prestigious [[Noether Lecture]] for the [[Association for Women in Mathematics]] in [[Phoenix, Arizona]].<ref name=AWM>{{cite web |title=Mary F. Wheeler - Large Scale Modeling of Problems Arising in Flow in Porous Media - Phoenix, Arizona 1989 |url=http://www.awm-math.org/noetherbrochure/Wheeler89.html |work=Profiles of Women in Mathematics: The Emmy Noether Lectures |publisher=Association for Women in Mathematics |year=2005 |accessdate=13 October 2013 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20100612232327/http://awm-math.org/noetherbrochure/Wheeler89.html |archive-date=12 June 2010 |url-status=dead }}</ref> Her talk was titled "Large Scale Modeling of Problems Arising in Flow in Porous Media".<ref name=AWM />
